intro: Psychoneuroendocrinology studies how hormones and the brain act on each other. This entry covers how hormone release is controlled from hypothalamus to target gland (Tables 33-6 and 33-7), organizational and activational effects in development, and how endocrine function is assessed. It then follows each axis and hormone in turn: the adrenal stress axis and its changes in Cushing syndrome, Addison disease and depression; gonadal steroids, testosterone and DHEA; estrogen and progesterone, premenstrual dysphoric disorder and menopause; the thyroid axis; growth hormone; prolactin; and melatonin, oxytocin and insulin. Update boxes add what later trials showed about estrogen and dementia, testosterone for women, the dexamethasone suppression test and intranasal insulin.
objectives: Trace hormone control from the hypothalamus through the pituitary to target glands, and classify hormones by structure and mode of action.
Describe the HPA axis findings in depression, Cushing syndrome and Addison disease and what they mean for prognosis.
Summarize what is reported about testosterone, DHEA and the cortisol/DHEA ratio in mood, cognition and stress.
Explain the effects of estrogen on the brain and the features of premenstrual dysphoric disorder and perimenopause.
Recognize the psychiatric presentations of thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia and growth hormone disturbance.
Identify which endocrine claims in the chapter later trials did not confirm.
